title: Delhi's New Liquor App Allows Online Ordering, But Not Home Delivery
excerpt: DSIIDC's Delhi Liquor Booking app lets buyers browse, pay online and reserve bottles at 208 outlets — but they must collect in person within 48 hours, with no delivery option.
body:
• Delhi residents can now browse brands, check stock and pricing, and pay online through a new liquor booking app developed by the Delhi State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation (DSIIDC).
  • The catch is clear: there is no home delivery. Orders must be collected in person from the chosen DSIIDC outlet within 48 hours, using a QR code issued after payment.
  • Users must be at least 25 years old, and orders are capped at up to nine litres of whisky or 18 litres of beer per transaction.
  • For a Diwali party, time the order around the pickup: an order placed too early will fall outside the 48-hour collection window, and returns are not allowed once bottles are collected.

Delhi residents planning a Diwali party can now secure liquor in advance through a newly launched mobile application, but the purchase still ends with a trip to the shop. According to Mirror Now, the platform developed by the Delhi State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation, or DSIIDC, allows users to browse brands, select quantities and pay online before visiting a store for collection. Officials have clarified that the service does not include home delivery.

The catch: online payment, in-store pickup

That distinction matters for anyone reading "order online" as doorstep delivery. Customers are required to visit their chosen DSIIDC-operated retail outlet to pick up their items within a 48-hour window after the transaction is completed. Upon payment, users receive a QR code, which must be presented at the store to finalize the collection. TeluguNow reported the same limits: 208 DSIIDC stores, no home delivery, and pickup within 48 hours of online payment.

The application is designed to mitigate long queues and reduce congestion at payment counters. By allowing customers to check stock and pricing ahead of time, DSIIDC hopes to create a more efficient and transparent shopping experience. That is the practical gain for a party host: brand, quantity and payment are settled before the store visit, so pickup should be shorter than a conventional purchase made entirely at the counter during the festive rush.

Who can order, and how much

The service is currently available exclusively at the 208 retail outlets managed by DSIIDC, which Mirror Now described as one of four government bodies authorized to sell liquor in the capital. It is not, on the reporting available, a citywide service covering every government outlet. A host whose usual vend is run by another corporation should not assume that shop will appear in the app.

Eligibility and quantity are also built into the system. To comply with local excise regulations, users must be at least 25 years old to access the app. The system enforces legal purchase limits, allowing individuals to order up to nine litres of whisky or 18 litres of beer per transaction.

Cancellation and returns are not symmetrical. The platform offers cancellation for orders not yet picked up, but officials noted that returns are not permitted once the product has been collected. Check brands, sizes and quantities carefully before paying, and again at the counter, because a mistake discovered after collection cannot be returned under the reported terms.

How to use it for a Diwali party

The sourced steps are straightforward. Browse the brands, choose a DSIIDC shop, select bottle sizes and quantities, and pay online. Save the QR code issued after payment, because it must be presented at the store, and collect from that outlet within 48 hours. If plans change before pickup, use the cancellation feature; do not treat collection as a point at which an unwanted bottle can still be sent back.

For Diwali specifically, the 48-hour rule is the planning constraint. Ordering well in advance risks the collection window closing before the pickup trip; ordering at the last moment removes the queue benefit the app was built to provide. The useful middle ground, on the reported rules, is to order close enough to the party that collection falls comfortably inside the two days after payment.

What happens next

Whether the app expands will depend on use. Since the launch, uptake has been described by officials as lukewarm. DSIIDC is monitoring consumer engagement, and any expansion or additional features will be contingent on how effectively the public adopts the current model. For this Diwali, the offer is narrower than the headline suggests: online browsing, online payment and a shorter pickup — not liquor delivered to the door.
